differences.title: 1. PURPOSE
differences.leftDesc: WebAuthn verifies who you are by using public-key credentials and a challenge from the relying party. Successful verification proves possession and origin constraints, not just a session cookie.
differences.rightDesc: OAuth 2.0 enables third-party applications to request access to protected resources. It focuses on delegation via tokens and scopes rather than performing a browser login ceremony by itself.

differences.title: 2. CRYPTO PRIMITIVES
differences.leftDesc: WebAuthn credentials are asymmetric keys. Authenticators sign a server-provided challenge (and context) with the private key; the server verifies using the stored public key and checks signature counters.
differences.rightDesc: OAuth access tokens are typically opaque or JWT-like bearer strings. Possession of the token grants API access, so practical security depends on token audience, scope, lifetime, transport security, and revocation strategy.

differences.title: 3. SERVER-SIDE VERIFICATION
differences.leftDesc: Server verifies an assertion: RP ID binding, client data origin, challenge match, and signature validity against the credential public key. It may also enforce user verification and handle replay via challenges.
differences.rightDesc: Authorization servers issue tokens after consent/auth flows. Resource servers validate them by verifying JWT signatures (if JWT) or calling introspection/using middleware to confirm expiry, scope, and issuer.

differences.title: 4. THREAT MODEL FIT
differences.leftDesc: WebAuthn binds authentication to a specific domain (RP ID) and leverages origin checks, so stolen passwords are irrelevant. The protocol constrains replay and mitigates credential stuffing.
differences.rightDesc: OAuth addresses risks around over-scoping and confused deputy problems. Security comes from correct client registration, redirect URI handling, scope minimization, and short-lived tokens.

differences.title: 5. TOKEN/ARTIFACT SHAPE
differences.leftDesc: WebAuthn primarily exchanges structured JSON (registration and assertion objects) plus challenge/response data. During registration, attestation can provide provenance evidence of authenticator properties.
differences.rightDesc: OAuth defines access tokens and optionally refresh tokens. The actual token format is implementation-specific, but contracts include token type, expiry, and claims like aud/scope/iss when JWT is used.

differences.title: 6. USER EXPERIENCE FLOW
differences.leftDesc: Authentication is a two-step ceremony: the server sends a challenge, the browser asks the authenticator to sign, then the browser posts the assertion for verification. No third-party token grants are required.
differences.rightDesc: OAuth commonly uses browser redirects and grant types (e.g., Authorization Code). The user authenticates with the authorization server, then the client receives tokens via a back-channel exchange.

differences.title: 7. DEPLOYMENT & INTEGRATION
differences.leftDesc: WebAuthn requires registering credentials per user and storing public keys and credential metadata. You must configure RP ID, supported algorithms, and policies like user verification and resident keys.
differences.rightDesc: OAuth requires an authorization server, client registrations, redirect URI validation, and resource server token verification. Integration typically involves middleware or gateways to enforce scopes and audiences.
